title: What the Retail Greeting ‘Welcome in’ Says About What Customers Really Want
summary: The phrase has started showing up everywhere. It reveals a lot about our discomforts with both human and robotic interactions.
body_markdown:

Walk into an American store these days and there is every chance that the first thing you hear will be: “Welcome in.” This phrase has become a coast-to-coast mainstay; there is a whole yearslong trail of[news](https://www.wsj.com/business/welcome-in-the-two-word-greeting-thats-taking-over-and-driving-shoppers-nuts-8443421f)[articles](https://www.washingtonpost.com/style/trends/2025/11/28/welcome-in-retail-greeting/) and[internet](https://www.reddit.com/r/asklinguistics/comments/zuogcd/when_did_welcome_in_become_a_common_greeting_in_a/)[posts](https://www.reddit.com/r/asklinguistics/comments/bkma3b/welcome_vs_welcome_in/?utm_source=share&utm_medium=ios_app&utm_name=iossmf) chronicling its spread. Some businesses specifically instruct employees to say it. (When the academic[Victor H. Mair noticed it](https://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu/nll/?p=65880) , at a Wyoming truck stop in 2024, workers happily confirmed that it was standard policy.) Some employees pick it up on their own. (It’s also common among video streamers greeting new viewers.) Some customers do not notice it at all, until the day they suddenly *do* and begin hearing it everywhere.


It’s not a new phrase — you can find “welcome in” in 19th-century texts (“The porter said, ‘[Welcome, welcome in](https://books.google.de/books?id=ZhEEAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA294&dq=%22welcome+in%22&hl=de&sa=X&ved=0ahUKEwibg9irr7HfAhUFy6QKHUAhAC4Q6AEIOzAE#v=onepage&q=%22welcome%20in%22&f=false) ,’ and opened the gate”) or infer it from punny old business names (the Welcome Inn) — but *something* clearly happened, this century, to send it surging through American commerce.


There are people who dislike this for business reasons. Bob Phibbs, a retail strategist, has written that “welcome in” makes sense in hospitality — say, while guiding a guest to a restaurant table — but is “[retail’s equivalent of a shrug](https://www.retaildoc.com/blog/welcome-in-isnt-a-greeting-its-a-sales-killer) ,” ending conversations instead of starting to make a sale. Another retail specialist, Kit Campoy, wrote on LinkedIn that she trained employees *not* to use it, giving them a much taller order: “In my store, we taught our team to use natural greetings. Like a human. Like a friend. Greet someone like you know them.”


Then there are those who dislike “welcome in” for linguistic reasons: It strikes them as odd and stilted, bizarre store jargon. The “in” does feel naggingly superfluous; what is it contributing that “welcome” does not already cover? My suspicion, at first, was that a stand-alone “welcome” struck people as quaint, fusty or formal, a weird curtsy of a word, so they were tweaking its mouthfeel to echo more everyday phrases: welcome *back* , welcome *home* , welcome *aboard* . Then I saw a commenter on the excellent Language Log blog expressing his amazement that the addition of “in” somehow made “welcome” *more* formal. It turns out people have radically different readings of “welcome in” — to some it’s warm and folksy, to others prim or bland or (as one sommelier told The Wall Street Journal) “just kind of extra.”


It’s fun to tease out these varying impressions, and possibly less fun to think about why we hear the same words in different stores. Sometimes the answer is “aggressive training.” Each business aims to set a particular tone, often one that’s inviting, accommodating, friendly. Each business also understands that its human employees are not reliably ** brimming with warmth, enthusiasm and a tireless commitment to customer satisfaction, nor are they getting paid enough to put much effort into faking it. But there are some things you can script, letting the company speak directly to customers through the mouths of its hirelings.


There’s a whole fascinating wealth of academic literature on this process; it’s the source of the much-abused term “emotional labor,” which originally referred to the actorly performance of service roles. Ritz-Carlton hotels, the inspiration for the word “ritzy,” have embraced unusually formal language: no “I’m sorry” or “you’re welcome,” only “please accept my apology” and “my pleasure.” A[2002 Harvard Business Review article](https://hbr.org/2002/06/my-week-as-a-room-service-waiter-at-the-ritz) captured new hires’ being asked to repeat the word “no” before being told: “That is the last time you should use that word in this hotel.” There was a similar rejection of negativity in an Apple Store training workbook[leaked to Gizmodo in 2012](https://gizmodo.com/how-to-be-a-genius-this-is-apples-secret-employee-trai-5938323) . Computers couldn’t “crash” or have “bugs” or become “hot” (only “stop responding” or experience “issues” or grow “warm”), and workers were never to apologize for the technology: The correct response to a catastrophic drive failure was something like “I’m sorry you’re feeling frustrated,” which you’d think would have cost Apple dearly in compensation for on-the-job punchings. Collect all this language in one place and it looks hilariously manipulative, like the notebook of a budding sociopath.
